QF.id: AIFM CII Investment Process and Governance_23

question.text: A Shareholders' Agreement (SHA) is typically required alongside the SSA because:

answer.text: The SHA is signed only by the AIF and the investment banker
The SSA binds only the company, not the existing shareholders; the SHA binds all existing shareholders to the agreed rights and obligations
SEBI regulations mandate a separate SHA for every AIF investment
The SHA replaces the Articles of Association entirely

explanation.text: The Logic: SSA is between company and AIF — hence binds the company only. The SHA is an inter-se agreement among ALL existing shareholders, binding them to the new rights/obligations (tag-along, drag-along, ROFR, affirmative rights, etc.). Without SHA, other shareholders could simply ignore the AIF's rights. The Trap: SEBI doesn't mandate SHAs. SHA doesn't replace AOA; rather the AOA is amended to mirror the SHA. Investment banker is not party. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C tests this. Articles amendment is a standard step — failure to amend AOA is a common ground for dispute. Manager's Pro-Tip: Always amend the AOA to incorporate SHA-protected provisions (especially tag/drag/affirmative) — Indian law gives AOA overriding effect over SHA in conflicts, so unmirrored SHA rights may be unenforceable against third parties.
